item.title: Lecture 06
item.description:
🚨 Caution
  • Bring about €0.30 next week for the new photocopies.
  • The teacher said there were about five classes left before the end of the year, with evaluations starting in January.
  • Certificate requirements include at least 80% attendance, class participation and evaluations.

Révision

Être & Avoir

  1. Conjugate these verbs.
Singular Subject Plural Subject Être (Singular) Être (Plural) Avoir (Singular) Avoir (Plural)
Je Nous suis sommes ai avons
Tu Vous es êtes as avez
Il Ils est sont a ont
Elle Elles est sont a ont

  1. Make a full sentence with each subject pronoun and each verb.

    Être

    • Je suis étudiant.
    • Nous sommes étudiants.
    • Tu es français.
    • Vous êtes colombien.
    • Il est timide.
    • Ils sont riches.
    • Elle est calme.
    • Elles sont optimistes.

    Avoir

    • J’ai un ordinateur.
    • Nous avons un stylo.
    • Tu as une mère.
    • Vous avez deux tantes.
    • Il a une fille.
    • Elle a un mobile.
    • Ils ont un frère.
    • Elles ont une femme.

  2. Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dans ton sac ?

    • Dans mon sac, il y a un ordinateur, un stylo et un livre.

  3. Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dans la salle de classe ?

    • Dans la salle de classe, il y a des tables.

  4. Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dans une famille typique ?

    • Il y a un père, une mère, un fils et une fille dans une famille typique.

  5. Qui est dans la salle de classe ?

    • Dans la salle de classe, il y a un professeur et des étudiants.

Revision Reminders

  • Keep sentences simple; reuse nationality, personality, family and classroom vocabulary.
  • Use être for nationality, profession and personality; use avoir for possessions and age.
  • Check verb spelling and adjective agreement, especially plural -s.
  • Distinguish ils sont / ils ont and un / une when speaking.
  • Qu’est-ce qu’il y a… ? asks what is there; Qui est… ? asks who is there.
  • If stuck, move to the next item and return later. Listen to classmates and check whether you understand them.

Numbers — Revision

  • Reviewed the numbers on page 04, mainly up to 69.
Number French
30 trente
40 quarante
50 cinquante
60 soixante
  • Add et un for 31, 41, 51, 61; other units normally follow without et.
  • 70 = 60 + 10; 71 = 60 + 11. These were introduced briefly; further practice will follow.
  • Know how to say a number, even when writing it as digits.
Examples
  • 31 — trente et un
  • 43 — quarante-trois
  • 61 — soixante et un
  • 69 — soixante-neuf
  • 70 — soixante-dix
  • 71 — soixante et onze

Possessive Adjectives

The way of showing possession:

  1. Use Avoir
Examples

J’ai un sac.

  1. Use De
Examples

Le frère de Jasmine s’appelle Thomas. Son frère s’appelle Thomas.

  1. Use Possessive Adjectives
Examples

Mon frère s’appelle Thomas.

Possessive Adjectives

  • The owner determines the row; the following noun determines gender and number.
  • son / sa / ses can all mean his or her.
  • Use ton / ta / tes when addressing one person with tu; use votre / vos for a group or someone addressed formally with vous.
  • Mon ami / Mon amie sound the same; a name or context may clarify who is meant.
Singular Subject Masculine (Sg.) Feminine (Sg.) Plural English Plural Subject Masculine (Sg.) Feminine (Sg.) Plural English
Je mon ma mes my Nous notre notre nos our
Tu ton ta tes your Vous votre votre vos your
Il son sa ses his Ils leur leur leurs their
Elle son sa ses her Elles leur leur leurs their
Examples
  • Mon ami s’appelle Thomas.
  • Ma sœur s’appelle Caroline.
  • Mon amie s’appelle Sarah. ↪Use mon/ton/son before a feminine singular noun beginning with a vowel or a silent h.
Practice
  • Mon frère est étudiant.
  • Mon sac a trois stylos.
  • Ma mère a un ordinateur.
  • Ma tante a un frère.
  • Mes amis ne sont pas étudiants.
  • Il y a trois personnes dans ma famille.

Writing Practice — Two Friends

  • Write two separate paragraphs, one about a male friend and one about a female friend: 3–4 sentences each.
  • Include name, nationality and personality.
  • Start with Mon ami / Mon amie, then use il / elle consistently.
  • Check the verb and the gender and number of adjectives.
  • et is never followed by liaison.
📝 Practice — Male Friend

Mon ami s’appelle Thomas. Il est français. Il est timide, mais optimiste.

📝 Practice — Female Friend

Mon amie s’appelle Sarah. Elle est maltaise. Elle est sociable et responsable.

Simple Questions

Ways of Asking Yes / No Questions

📝 Learning Priority

Focus on intonation and Est-ce que. For now, recognise inversion when you hear it; producing it fluently is not required.

  1. Just Use Intonation
    • Keep the statement order: S + V + O.
    • Statement ↘ / Question ↗
Examples
  • Ton ami s’appelle Thomas ?
  • Tes amis s’appellent Thomas et Sarah ? ↪ Liaison: tes [z] amis.
  • Ton amie s’appelle Sarah ?
  1. Use Est-ce que + S + V + O
    • Introduce a yes / no question without changing the statement order.
📝 Notes

Est-ce que is never used alone; follow it with a clause. Est-ce que + il → Est-ce qu’il. Do not omit the verb: Est-ce que introduces the question; it does not replace the sentence’s verb.

Examples
  • Est-ce que ta famille a trois personnes ?
    • Oui, il y a trois personnes dans ma famille.
  • Est-ce qu’il y a un stylo dans ton sac ?
    • Non, il y a trois stylos dans mon sac.
  1. Use Inversion
    • Place the verb before the subject pronoun: V + S + O.
    • Join the verb and subject pronoun with a hyphen.
Examples
  • Vous êtes français. → Êtes-vous français ?
  • Tu as un stylo. → As-tu un stylo ?
📝 Page 09

Il y a… → Y a-t-il… ? — Recognise this inverted question form on the vocabulary sheet.

Question Practice

  • Turn sentences about your friends into questions using intonation, then Est-ce que.
  • When asking someone else, adjust mon / ma / mes → ton / ta / tes as appropriate.
  • The teacher noted that intonation can sound more natural when confirming something you think you already know; this is a matter of context, not a ban on Est-ce que to ask something.
📝 Practice — Male Friend

Intonation

  • Ton ami s’appelle Thomas ?
  • Il est français ?
  • Il est timide, mais optimiste ?

Est-ce que

  • Est-ce que ton ami s’appelle Thomas ?
  • Est-ce qu’il est français ?
  • Est-ce qu’il est timide, mais optimiste ?
📝 Practice — Female Friend

Intonation

  • Ton amie s’appelle Sarah ?
  • Elle est maltaise ?
  • Elle est sociable et responsable ?

Est-ce que

  • Est-ce que ton amie s’appelle Sarah ?
  • Est-ce qu’elle est maltaise ?
  • Est-ce qu’elle est sociable et responsable ?

Words & Text

📝 Tasks
  • Memorise the vocabulary on page 09 of the handout.
  • Read the text on page 10 of the handout.
  • Review today’s possessive adjectives and question forms.

Page 10 — Notes

  • Notice possession with de, question forms and où — where. Prepositions will be studied later.
  • Pronunciation of Mercier

Mercier ↪ie: ié

Notes
  • Mercier — /mɛʁ.sje/.
  • Perrier: do not pronounce the final r.
  • Voici / Voilà
    • Voici + noun — Here is / here are;
    • Voilà + noun — There is / there are;
    • Both can introduce people. Voici points to “here”; voilà points to “there”.
    • Voilà ! can also be used alone when showing or finding something — “There it is!”
Examples
  • Voici mon livre.
  • Voilà mon frère.
  • Voici mes amis.

item.title: Lecture 02
item.description:
🚨 Caution
  • Pay €0.25 for photocopies next week.
  • 4 November: possibly no class — to be confirmed.
  • 16 December: last class before the holiday break.
  • 6 January: expected return — to be confirmed.

Review

Pronunciation

Les salutations

  • Je m’appelle XXX.

Les voyelles

  • Vowels: a, e, i, o, u.

  • e

    • e: usually silent at the end of a word;
    • è: /ɛ/;
    • é: /e/.

    e.g. étudiante / étudiant.

Les consonnes

  • Final consonants are usually silent; C, R, F, L are often pronounced. e.g. Salut.

Spelling and Pronunciation

Spelling Rule Example
c c + a, o, u → /k/; c + e, i, y → /s/ ca → /ka/
ç — cedilla ç + a, o, u → /s/ Ça va ? /sa va/ — How are you?
¨ — tréma Marks a vowel pronounced separately; used on ë, ï, ü. Noël /nɔ.ɛl/ — Christmas
ˆ — circumflex Used on â, ê, î, ô, û; may mark a historical s. hôpital — hospital; compare hospital
Double consonants double consonant → usually one consonant sound Bernadette /bɛʁ.na.dɛt/ — tt → /t/

Tu / Vous — You

  • tu — informal; one person.
  • vous — formal for one person; any group of people.

Alphabet

French Alphabet With Native Audio

  • Accents are part of spelling; name them when spelling a word aloud.
French English
accent aigu — é acute accent
accent grave — è grave accent
accent circonflexe — ˆ circumflex
tréma — ¨ diaeresis
cédille — ç cedilla
majuscule capital letter
minuscule lowercase letter
apostrophe — ’ apostrophe
trait d’union — - hyphen
Examples
  • Comment s’écrit votre nom ? — How is your name spelled?

Grammar and Vocabulary

Subject Pronouns

Singular Plural
je — I nous — we
tu — you (familiar singular) vous — you (familiar plural; formal singular and plural)
il — he; it (masculine) ils — they (masculine or mixed gender)
elle — she; it (feminine) elles — they (feminine)
on — one; you; people; we; they
  • Subject + verb + complement: normally keep the subject in a French statement.
  • ils → male or mixed group; elles → all-female group.
  • on → leave detailed usage for later.

Être — To Be

Singular Plural
je suis — I am nous sommes — we are
tu es — you are vous -(z)- êtes /vu zett/ — you are
il est — he / it is ils sont — they are
elle est — she / it is elles sont — they are
on est — one is / we are
  • vous êtes → /vu.zɛt/: liaison s → /z/.
  • il / ils and elle / elles sound the same in isolation; the verb can distinguish them: il est / ils sont.

Adjectifs — Adjectives

Nationalities

  • Nationality ≠ country: chinois — Chinese; Chine — China.
  • Nationality adjectives agree with the subject in gender and number.
Masculine Feminine English
maltais maltaise Maltese
français française French
chinois chinoise Chinese

Adjectives

  • Many adjectives below end in -e → same masculine and feminine form: riche, optimiste, responsable.
Adjective English Contrast English
riche rich pauvre poor
optimiste optimistic pessimiste pessimistic
responsable responsible irresponsable irresponsible
facile easy difficile difficult
sociable sociable / outgoing timide shy
calme calm hyper hyperactive
magnifique magnificent / wonderful ridicule ridiculous
  • agréable — pleasant / nice.
  • hyper is informal. The last three pairs are contrasts, rather than exact opposites.
Examples
  • Je m’appelle Jingyuan. Je suis chinois et optimiste. — My name is Jingyuan. I am Chinese and optimistic.
  • Il s’appelle Paul. Il est français et sociable. — His name is Paul. He is French and outgoing.
  • Elle s’appelle Maria. Elle est maltaise et calme. — Her name is Maria. She is Maltese and calm.
  • Je suis pauvre, mais optimiste. — I am poor but optimistic.
  • Nous sommes chinois. — We are Chinese: male or mixed group.
  • Nous sommes chinoises. — We are Chinese: all-female group.

Useful Words and Expressions

French English
et and
mais but
C’est vrai. That’s true.
Non. No.
Qui ? /ki/ Who?
Qui est-ce ? Who is it? / Who is this?
Il s’appelle… His name is…
Je ne sais pas. I don’t know.
parce que because
car because / for
  • C’est + name → identify a person; il / elle est + adjective → describe a person.
Examples
  • Qui est-ce ? — C’est Paul. / Il s’appelle Paul. — Who is it? — It’s Paul. / His name is Paul.
  • Il est français et sociable. — He is French and outgoing.

Practice

  • Spell your name; let a partner write it, then switch.
  • Introduce yourself and a partner: name + nationality + adjective.
  • Practise affirmative sentences first; learn expressions as complete phrases.

item.title: Lecture 01
item.description:
General

Contacts

Email: Bernadette.ann.grech@lifelonglearing.edu.mt Coordinator’s Email: Pierre.Tonna.2@lifelonglearing.edu.mt Coordinator’s Mobile No.: 99891208

How to be successful in the course?

  1. Come to Class.
  2. 80% attendance minimum for a certificate (approximately six absences; unconfirmed).
  3. Arrive on time: the first ten minutes include revision and announcements.

What is important?

  • Follow the rules!
  • Assessments have fixed dates, to be announced—not only in May.
  • 10 tests; the best 8 grades count. Eight supplementary tasks were also mentioned; details need confirmation.
  • Most assessments: no notes, phones or computers.
  • Most teaching is planned to be completed by around February.
  • Review what we have learned; master the assigned vocabulary before moving ahead.
  • Bring printed handouts.
  • Exchange contact details with a classmate for missed work.
  • Follow the class materials; Duolingo is not discourages at this stage expect individual word pronunciation lookups.
  • Holidays follow the government school calendar.

Greeting

  • Je m’appelle Bernadette.

    • Why? /Pourquoi?
    • Français?
    • When? Quand?

  • Bonsoir

    • Good evening.

  • Bonjour — Hello; daytime greeting.

  • Salut ! — Hi / bye; informal.

  • Au revoir / À bientôt / À demain — Goodbye / See you soon / See you tomorrow.

  • Comment vas-tu ? / Comment allez-vous ? — How are you? Informal singular / formal singular or plural.

  • Ça va ? — How’s it going?

  • Ça va bien. / Je vais bien. / Très bien, merci. — I’m fine. / Very well, thank you.

  • Comment t’appelles-tu ? / Comment vous appelez-vous ? — What is your name? Informal / formal.

  • Je suis… — I am…

  • Enchanté(e). — Nice to meet you.

  • Madame / Monsieur / Mademoiselle — Madam / sir / miss (traditional title).

  • Introductions: give your name, then explain in English why you are learning French and any previous study.

How to pronounce?

Vowels & Constants Letters

Vowels A, E, I, O, U
Constants B, C, D, …etc

Example:

  • **Bonsoir
  • **
  • J==e== m’appell==e==
  • Salut

Final Consonants

If last constant is C R F L ,it will be pronounced

  • This is a general rule with exceptions; other final consonants are generally silent, e.g. salut (t), Nicolas (s).
  • Check word endings first and lightly cross out silent letters on handouts.
Examples
  • Parc
  • Car
  • Surf
  • il

Different type of ’e'

  1. e silent e
  2. è |aay|
  3. é |ay| |ā|
  • Final e is often silent; unaccented e is not silent everywhere.
  • è /ɛ/ and é /e/ are different sounds; practise with the teacher’s examples.
📝 Notes

A final silent e can make the preceding silent consonant pronounced.

  • Étudiant → Étudiante: t becomes pronounced.
  • Louis → Louise: s becomes pronounced.
  • Pascal → Pascale: Same pronunciation (l is already pronounced).
  • Simon → Simone: The nasal vowel changes and n becomes pronounced.
  • Étudiant / Étudiante — Male / female student.

Nasal Vowels

  • A, I, O, U + N / M → Nasal sound

    • A basic spelling guide, with exceptions: n / m is not pronounced separately in these nasal sounds.
Examples
  • bien — good / well
  • faim — hunger
  • question / questions — question / questions

Liaison

  • In certain phrases, a normally silent final consonant links to the next vowel sound. Practise whole phrases as well as individual words.

Tu / Vous — You

Tu / Toi Vous
Formality Informal Formal or informal
Used with Friends, family, people you know Strangers, people you respect, or groups
Number Singular (1 person) Singular (1) or Plural (≥2)
  • Tu — Informal, singular only.
  • Vous — Formal for one person; used for two or more people regardless of formality.
  • Toi — Stressed form of tu (you).
Examples

Et toi ? — And you? Et vous ? — And you? (formal or plural)

  • Use vous when unsure, especially with strangers, older people or authority figures.
  • Et toi ? / Et vous ? returns a question without repeating it in full.

Cognates vs. False Cognates

  • Cognates — Words with a common origin.

  • False Cognates — Similar-looking words with different origins.

  • False Friends / Faux Amis — Similar-looking words with different meanings.

  • e.g. question means the same in both languages; French car means because, not a vehicle.

🚨 Caution

You cannot assume that all similar-looking words share the same meaning.

L1 Exercise

  1. Bonjour, madame.
  2. Salut!
  3. Au revoir, monsieur.
  4. Au revoir, madame.
